title: Rapid escalation protocols and runbook bootstrap
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Summary
-------
This page defines a standardized rapid-escalation protocol, a 90-minute runbook bootstrap process for newly onboarded services, and reusable customer-communication templates for the status page and direct emails. It is intended for SREs, on-call engineers, and product liaisons who must stabilize incidents quickly and consistently while preserving post-incident learning.

Principles
----------
- Safety first: protect customer data and avoid actions that increase blast radius.
- Fast stabilization over perfect diagnosis: prioritize mitigations that restore customer-visible behavior.
- Clear ownership: assign Incident Commander (IC) and Comm Lead within 5 minutes.
- Post-incident learning: every incident must have a timeline and a 5-point action plan in the postmortem.

Incident severity definitions (for escalation decisions)
----------------------------------------------------
- Sev 1 (Critical): Global production outage or p99 latency > 10s for > 5 minutes, or error rate > 5% for critical API routes, impacting majority of customers.
- Sev 2 (High): Large subset of traffic affected, p99 latency > 3s or error rate > 1% for > 10 minutes, partial feature loss.
- Sev 3 (Medium): Single-region or small percentage of users affected, degraded experience.
- Sev 4 (Low): Internal tooling or non-customer-facing degradation.

Quantitative thresholds (examples - service teams should customize)
------------------------------------------------------------------
- Request success rate threshold: 99.0% per minute (if crossed -> alert escalation).
- P99 latency threshold: 3000 ms (if crossed -> paging for Sev2).
- Queue length growth threshold: 2x baseline sustained for 5 minutes.
- CPU/GPU utilization: > 90% sustained for 10m on primary nodes = investigate scaling.

Roles and responsibilities
--------------------------
- Incident Commander (IC): Owns triage decisions, runbook execution, and timeline.
- Communications Lead (Comm Lead): Publishes status updates, coordinates external comms.
- Tech Leads / Service Owners: Provide domain context and approve rollbacks.
- SRE responder(s): Execute mitigations (scaling, cache flushes, rollback).
- Product Liaison: Triage customer impact and prioritize remediation.

Rapid escalation checklist (first 15 minutes)
-------------------------------------------
1. Acknowledge alert and identify scope: which services/customers/regions?
2. Assign roles (IC + Comm Lead) and create incident channel (Slack / #incident-<id>).
3. Post initial status on internal channel: what we see, who’s on it, SLO impact.
4. Triage using Top-5 checks below.
5. If impact matches Sev1/Sev2, page additional responders and invoke schedule for escalation.

Top-5 triage checks (order matters)
----------------------------------
1. Is the service healthy? 
   - curl -sSf https://service.example.internal/health || true
   - kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=service -o wide
2. Are errors increasing in the last 5 minutes?
   - Datadog query / Loki query example (replace service name):
     - datadog: query 'avg(last_5m):anomalies(avg:trace.errors{service:service},"basic",2, direction="both")'
     - loki: {app="service"} |~ "ERROR" | count_over_time(5m)
3. Latency and QPS checks:
   - Grafana dashboard: Service > Latency (p50/p95/p99), QPS.
4. Resource health (nodes, disk, network):
   - kubectl top nodes | grep -E "(cpu|memory)"
   - check cloud provider console for disk pressure / network egress spikes.
5. Recent deploys or config changes in last 30 minutes:
   - git log --since='30 minutes' --oneline deploy/manifest
   - CI/CD dashboard: check recent pipeline failures or rollouts.

Immediate mitigations (choose the least invasive first)
-------------------------------------------------------
- Scale up replicas / add burst capacity: kubectl scale deployment/service --replicas=<n>
- Enable read-only mode or degraded feature path to reduce write pressure.
- Rollback latest deploy using the orchestration console or: kubectl rollout undo deployment/service
- Temporarily increase timeouts and circuit breaker thresholds at the gateway for graceful degradation.
- DNS/traffic split rollback: revert weighted routing to previous stable version.
- Cache warm-up: invalidate stale caches carefully (avoid thundering herd).

Safe rollback checklist
-----------------------
1. Confirm the last successful image or git tag.
2. Verify rollbacks in a small canary (if platform supports).
3. Announce the rollback start and expected duration in incident channel.
4. Monitor health metrics continuously during rollback (p50/p99, error rate, 5xx).
5. After rollback, validate with synthetic checks before closing incident.

90-minute runbook bootstrap for a new service
-------------------------------------------
Goal: produce a minimal production runbook and on-call checklist that an on-call engineer can follow during first incidents. Timebox: 90 minutes.

Pre-steps (prior to 90 minutes)
- Ensure service repository and deployment manifests are accessible.
- Service owner present or reachable.

0-10m: Set context
- Create a confluence child page under the service's runbooks folder. Title: "<service-name> - oncall runbook (bootstrap)".
- Copy this template into the page.

10-30m: Core diagnostics and dashboards
- Identify the main health endpoint and deploy pipeline. Paste the URLs into the runbook.
- Add links to primary Grafana dashboard all on-call will use.
- Add the alert definitions and thresholds (link to alert policy).

30-60m: Tiered mitigations and ownership
- Write 3 prioritized mitigations (scale, rollback, degrade).
- Document owners for each mitigation and add quick commands.
- Add escalation matrix: who to page for Tier 1, Tier 2, and product org.

60-80m: Communication templates and status page snippet
- Add copy for Status Page templates (see below).

80-90m: Validation and sign-off
- Walk through the runbook with service owner and SRE. Add expected on-call retention links (pager duty or rota).

Post-incident: timeline and postmortem requirements
--------------------------------------------------
- Timeline must include: detection time, IC assigned, mitigations applied, rollback time, resolution time, and customer impact summary.
- Postmortem required for Sev1/Sev2 within 7 business days. Postmortem must include: root cause hypothesis, evidence, action items with owners and due dates, and validation plan.
- Severity review: SRE lead and Product manager must concur on severity classification before publishing postmortem.

Game day (exercise) playbook (quarterly recommended)
---------------------------------------------------
1. Define scope: which service and which failure mode (eg. cross-region outage, database failover).
2. Pre-game checklist: notify stakeholders, ensure a dedicated Slack channel, and prepare monitoring snapshots.
3. Run the scenario with a single on-call team, record timestamps, and measure time-to-detect and time-to-restore.
4. Debrief within 24 hours, publish findings, and track improvements as action items.

Status page and customer comms templates
--------------------------------------
Use a triage-first cadence for public updates: initial notice within 30 minutes for Sev1/Sev2, follow-ups every 60 minutes until degraded state; then every 4 hours until resolved.

Template A — Initial incident (public status page)
Title: Degraded performance for <service-name> (investigating)\Body: We are experiencing degraded performance for <service-name> that may affect requests to <affected-endpoints>. Our engineering team is investigating. Current impact: <summary of customers/regions>. Next update: <time>.

Template B — Mitigation in progress (public status page)\Title: Performance degradation — mitigation in progress\Body: We have identified probable cause and are applying mitigations (scaled replicas / rolling back a recent deploy / enabling degraded mode). We expect to see improvement within <ETA>. We will update again at <time>.

Template C — Resolved\Title: Incident resolved — <service-name>\Body: The issue has been resolved as of <time>. Root cause (provisional): <one-line cause>. Customer impact: <summary>. Follow-up: a postmortem will be published after investigation.

Slack / internal status snippets
- Initial: [INCIDENT 1234] IC: @name — detected p99=4.5s on api.read. Assigned responders: @sre1 @sre2. Channel: #incident-1234.
- Public link: Status page URL (always include).

Email template (customer-facing, for major incidents)
Subject: Service impact to <service-name> — interim update\Body: Hello <customer>,
We’re currently investigating a service disruption affecting <service-name>. We have identified the likely cause and are working on mitigation. Current status: <brief impact>. Expected next update: <time>. Thank you for your patience.
Regards,
Redwood Inference Support

Postmortem template (required fields)
- Title, incident id, severity.
- Summary (1 paragraph).
- Timeline (minute-level).
- Root cause analysis (with evidence).
- Mitigations performed.
- Customer impact & compensation considerations (if any).
- Action items (owner, due date, verification steps).
- Post-deployment verification plan.

Metrics to publish in postmortem
- Mean time to detect (MTTD).
- Mean time to mitigate (MTTM).
- Mean time to restore (MTTR).
- Number of customers affected (approx).

Runbook hygiene and governance
-----------------------------
- Every runbook must have an owner and quarterly review date.
- Runbook pages older than 12 months without review will be flagged and assigned for refresh.
- Changes to runbooks that affect on-call steps require a game-day validation before the next rotation.

Appendix: quick command cheat sheet
----------------------------------
- Health check: curl -sSf https://service.example.internal/health || echo 'unhealthy'
- Pod status: kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=service -o wide
- Rollback: kubectl rollout undo deployment/service -n prod
- Force scale: kubectl scale deploy/service --replicas=5 -n prod
- Logs: loki query example: {app=\"service\"} |~ \"ERROR\" | tail 200

Ownership and escalation contact matrix (example)
------------------------------------------------
| Role | Primary contact | Secondary | Pager |
| Incident Commander | @ic-oncall | Tech Lead | SRE oncall rota |
| Communications Lead | @comm-lead | Customer Success rep | Support rota |
| DB / Storage Owner | @db-owner | @infra-lead | DB pager |

How to raise improvements to this page
-------------------------------------
If you identify gaps or better mitigations, please: 1) open a PR to update the runbook page, 2) add a reviewer from SRE, and 3) schedule a micro game-day to validate the change.

Notes and references
--------------------
- See also: Incident Command Playbook and Escalation Matrix (linked).
- SLO definitions and measurement guidance live in eng-sre > slo-and-error-budgets.
- This page is a bootstrap — teams should expand into service-specific runbooks with full diagnostic queries and contact lists.
